name: sbml-decomposition
title: SBML in Tellurium vs process-bigraph decomposition — a speed × accuracy × composability tradeoff
lead:
A methods comparison, not a biology result. One curated SBML metabolic model
(Teusink glycolysis, BioModels BIOMD0000000064, 17 floating species) is run along
a spectrum of implementations under one workspace, each measured on the same three
axes. The deliverable is a decision guide: which decomposition patterns to use,
which to avoid, and why.

at_a_glance.role: monolithic SBML in libroadrunner/CVODE — the speed + accuracy reference
same model, operator-split sub-steps through a store — isolates orchestration overhead + splitting error (mechanical split)
biological upper/lower seam as two coupled process nodes sharing a store — genuine composability
fully native process-bigraph RHS, no libroadrunner — the far pole, high fidelity + max substitutability
parameter ensemble of monoliths on Ray — the one arm where vivarium wins on wall-clock
cross-engine hybrid (Tellurium + native in one composite) — the composability existence proof a monolith cannot match

genuinely multi-rate composite (N independent monoliths, geometric intervals) — exercises + measures the process-bigraph event-heap scheduler from PR-270 (O(P log P) vs the stock scan's O(P^2)), bit-identical results, the one arm that stress-tests the scheduler instead of the biology

synthetic N-organ scaling knob (species=3N+1, shared blood pool) — stretches a monolithic libroadrunner/CVODE instance past the fixed 17-species model to its strain point (the compile is superlinear in reactions, ~O(N^1.64)). The honest end-to-end finding is that decomposition into N per-organ processes is NOT a free win — its build only reaches parity in the hundreds of species and its per-tick run overhead makes it slower end-to-end at every N measured; a structural build-vs-run trade, not a scaling victory

the ADVERSARIAL arm — a stochastic Gillespie-SSA agent-based Lotka-Volterra model (discrete individuals, not an ODE) and its deterministic mean-field SBML/Tellurium reduction. Answers the prior question the other arms assume away ("can an ABM even BE an SBML model?") with numbers; the reduction is valid only in the large-population limit (K=400; 4.9% max rel err, 0% extinction) and structurally breaks at small population (K=8; 94% of runs go extinct — which the ODE can never show — 68% max rel err). Breaks the naive "any model is an SBML model" claim

how_to_read:
Start with arm 1 (the reference), then read arms 2→4 as increasing decomposition
(watch accuracy degrade and composability rise), then arm 5 (the parallel win) and
arm 6 (the capability proof). The 3-way tradeoff figure and the decision table are
the deliverable.

glossary.definition: advancing subsets of a system separately over an interval then composing — introduces a splitting error that shrinks with the interval
framework time / total wall-clock from Composite.timing_summary(); the SHARE of time outside process invoke(), not the decomposition cost
the ability to substitute a submodel, couple through a shared store, mix engines, or wire across scales — what decomposition buys

biological_story:
The vehicle is yeast glycolysis (Teusink et al. 2000), a 17-species kinetic model
with a stiff phosphate/energy coupling and a square-root adenylate assignment rule.
It is not studied here for its biology — it is a well-characterized, moderately stiff
reaction network that exercises the numerical and structural stressors a decomposition
has to survive.

Read the arms as a spectrum. Arm 1 hands the whole SBML model to libroadrunner/CVODE
in one piece — fast, exact, opaque. Arm 2 keeps the same model but advances it in
operator-split sub-steps that exchange state through a vivarium store each coupling
interval; this is a mechanical split, and it reveals that splitting across the strong
energy coupling diverges while a weak-seam split converges. Arm 3 cuts the model along
a genuine biological seam (upper vs lower glycolysis at the aldolase/F16P boundary)
into two coupled process nodes that reconcile additively through the real
process-bigraph apply path — the first point where the model is genuinely composable.
Arm 4 discards libroadrunner entirely and integrates a hand-written native RHS, the
far pole of composability. Arm 5 fans the monolith out into a parameter ensemble on a
real parallel backend. Arm 6 is the punchline: a single composite running half in
libroadrunner and half in native Python, sharing one species store — the capability a
monolith can never offer.
question:
When you have a biochemical model available as SBML, when should you run it
monolithically in Tellurium (libroadrunner/CVODE), and when is it worth
decomposing it into vivarium / process-bigraph sub-processes? What does each
point on that spectrum cost in performance and accuracy, and what does
decomposition buy that a monolith structurally cannot provide?
hypothesis:
Along the spectrum monolithic Tellurium → operator-split → modular submodels →
fully-native process-bigraph, performance and accuracy degrade monotonically
(the monolith is fastest and the numerical reference), while composability —
substitutability, store-coupling, cross-engine and multi-scale wiring — rises.
No point dominates on all three axes, so the right choice is governed by whether
the composability a decomposition buys is worth its quantified speed/accuracy cost
for the task at hand.

executive.what_is_this:
A head-to-head of six ways to run the SAME SBML model — from a single
libroadrunner/CVODE integration to a fully hand-written process-bigraph network —
measured on speed, accuracy (vs the monolithic reference), and composability.
executive.verdict:
Decomposition is never free on speed or accuracy, but the monolith cannot be
composed. Monolithic Tellurium is the fastest and the numerical reference; every
decomposition adds orchestration overhead and operator-splitting error that
shrinks as the coupling interval shrinks. The payoff is strictly on the
composability axis: only the decomposed arms can substitute a submodel, couple
through a shared store, or mix engines (arm 6 runs half libroadrunner / half
native in one composite — a thing a single SBML model structurally cannot do).
The ensemble arm is the one place vivarium wins on wall-clock (7.5× via Ray on
16 cores), because libroadrunner does not release the GIL so only OS-process
parallelism helps.

decisions_needed.question: Promote the Teusink-glycolysis vertical slice to the oscillator + signaling-cascade models?
decisions_needed.context: The harness + six arm types are proven on one model; models 2-3 are repetitions driven by the discovery-engine frontier.

scientific_argument.main_claim:
On the implementation spectrum for an SBML model, speed and accuracy are best at
the monolithic pole and composability is best at the decomposed pole; the choice
is a tradeoff with no dominating point, and the quantified costs make the decision
rule explicit.
evidence_for: Monolithic Tellurium (arm 1) is the accuracy reference and matches direct libroadrunner to ~1e-6 on a shared time grid.

Operator-split (arm 2) and modular (arm 3) both show real operator-splitting error that shrinks monotonically with the coupling interval (arm 2: 0.587→0.067; arm 3: 0.468→0.100), confirming the error is controllable but non-zero.
Fully-native process-bigraph (arm 4) reproduces the reference to ~1e-7 with a hand-ported RHS — the far pole is achievable at high fidelity but hand-written.
Arm 6 runs a cross-engine hybrid (upper glycolysis in libroadrunner, lower glycolysis native) sharing one store — a composition a monolith cannot express — and reproduces arm 3 to 3.2e-7.
The ensemble arm (arm 5) achieves a real 7.5× speedup via Ray OS processes on 16 cores.
evidence_against: overhead_fraction (framework share of wall-clock) is HIGHEST for the monolith (~0.32) and lowest for the decomposed/native arms (~0.02-0.05) — a cheap process makes the framework look expensive, so 'framework share' is NOT the decomposition cost. The decomposition cost is the wall-clock ratio to monolithic plus absolute framework seconds.

At 17 species the scalar-dict vs numpy-array leaf choice is perf-irrelevant (arm 4 variants indistinguishable); the scalar-dict penalty is linear in element count and only bites at 100s-1000s of species.
caveats: Single model (Teusink glycolysis) so far; generalization to a stiff oscillator and a modular signaling cascade is the next increment.

A clean operator split (arm 2) was only possible across the weakly-coupled glycogen/trehalose sinks; splitting across the strong P/ATP/ADP energy coupling diverges — do not generalize arm 2's splitting error to arbitrary decompositions.

Mismatched-interval decompositions carry an O(P^2) multi-rate scheduler cost in pb ≤1.10.x; process-bigraph PR #270 (unmerged as of 2026-10-25) reduces it to ~O(P log P). Our arms use equal intervals, the cheap regime. Prefer equal coupling intervals today.

competing_frameworks.name: monolith-always
competing_frameworks.prediction: running the whole SBML model in Tellurium is always the right choice
competing_frameworks.discriminated_by: arm 6 — a cross-engine composition the monolith structurally cannot express; and arm 5 — the ensemble wall-clock win

competing_frameworks.name: decompose-always
competing_frameworks.prediction: process-bigraph decomposition is free / always worth it
competing_frameworks.discriminated_by: arms 2-4 — the measured, non-zero speed + accuracy cost of every decomposition vs the monolithic reference

studies.name: arm1-monolithic-tellurium
studies.title: Arm 1 — Monolithic Tellurium (reference)
studies.question: Does the whole SBML model, integrated in one libroadrunner/CVODE call through a single TelluriumProcess, reproduce the model's reference trajectory, and what is its performance baseline?

findings.summary: Matches direct libroadrunner to max_rel_err ~1e-6 on a shared grid (rtol 1e-6, atol 1e-9).

overhead_fraction ~0.32 (highest of all arms): the single CVODE call is so cheap that framework time dominates its share — framework SHARE is largest for the cheapest process, not the most decomposed.

Bulk-port binding (viva-tellurium bulk_species + Array species leaf, libroadrunner bulk C API) makes arm1 ~12% faster wall-clock, BIT-IDENTICAL (max abs trajectory diff 0.0). The win lands in total runtime, not overhead_fraction (which stays ~0.32) — a real speedup that doesn't move the framework SHARE, reinforcing that share != cost.

studies.claim: Monolithic Tellurium reproduces the reference to ~1e-6 and is the fastest arm — the speed + accuracy reference.

derived.insight: Matches direct libroadrunner to max_rel_err ~1e-6 on a shared grid (rtol 1e-6, atol 1e-9).

studies.name: arm2-operator-split
studies.title: Arm 2 — Operator-split Tellurium
studies.question: If the same model is advanced in operator-split sub-steps that exchange state through a vivarium store each coupling interval, how much orchestration overhead and splitting error does that add, and does the error shrink with the interval?

findings.summary: Coarse interval 0.1 → max_rel_err 0.587; fine interval 0.0125 → 0.067 (monotone convergence); provisional tolerance T=0.10.
AVOID generalizing: a clean split only worked across the weak glycogen/trehalose sinks. Splitting across the strong energy (P/ATP/ADP, sqrt adenylate rule) coupling diverges for all intervals.

studies.claim: Operator-splitting error is real and shrinks with the coupling interval (0.587 → 0.067); a clean split was only possible across the weakly-coupled glycogen/trehalose sinks — splitting across the strong P/ATP/ADP energy coupling diverges.

derived.insight: Coarse interval 0.1 → max_rel_err 0.587; fine interval 0.0125 → 0.067 (monotone convergence); provisional tolerance T=0.10.

studies.name: arm3-modular-submodels
studies.title: Arm 3 — Modular submodels (biological seam)
studies.question: If the model is partitioned along a biological seam (upper vs lower glycolysis at aldolase/F16P) into two coupled process nodes sharing a store, does it still reproduce the reference, and is this a genuine multi-process composition?

findings.summary: Two process nodes share one species store, reconciling additively through the bigraph apply path (verified: core.apply/reconcile sum the deltas, not a local loop). Reproduces the operator-split reference exactly.
coupling step 0.002 → max_rel_err 0.468; 0.0005 → 0.100 (T=0.15). Looser than arm 2 because this seam crosses the strong energy coupling; divergence is guarded to status=diverged.
overhead_fraction ~0.05 (far below the monolith's 0.32): the decomposed arm spends more wall-clock inside the processes, so the framework is a smaller share.

studies.claim: A biological-seam decomposition reproduces the reference (0.468 → 0.100 as the coupling step shrinks, T=0.15) as a GENUINE multi-process composition — the first point on the spectrum where the model is composable.

derived.insight: Two process nodes share one species store, reconciling additively through the bigraph apply path (verified: core.apply/reconcile sum the deltas, not a local loop). Reproduces the operator-split reference exactly.

studies.name: arm4-native-pbg
studies.title: Arm 4 — Fully native process-bigraph
studies.question: Can the glycolysis ODE network be reimplemented as native process-bigraph processes (no libroadrunner at runtime) at reference fidelity, and does the state leaf representation (scalar-dict vs numpy-array) matter for performance at this scale?

findings.summary: Native RHS (all 17 reactions + 3 sqrt adenylate rules) matches the reference to max_rel_err ~1.05e-7; scalar and array variants bitwise identical.

Scalar-dict vs numpy-array overhead_fraction indistinguishable (0.023 vs 0.022); per-process leaf-crossing ~6.8ms vs 6.7ms, swamped by the ~289ms LSODA integration. The scalar-dict framework tax is linear in element count and only matters at large state.

studies.claim: A fully native process-bigraph implementation reaches reference fidelity (~1e-7); at 17 species the scalar-dict-vs-array leaf choice is perf-irrelevant (only bites at 100s-1000s of species).

derived.insight: Native RHS (all 17 reactions + 3 sqrt adenylate rules) matches the reference to max_rel_err ~1.05e-7; scalar and array variants bitwise identical.

studies.name: arm5-ensemble-ray
studies.title: Arm 5 — Ensemble on Ray
studies.question: When many instances of the monolithic model are run as a parameter ensemble, does vivarium orchestration on a real parallel backend (Ray) deliver a genuine throughput speedup?

findings.summary: n_instances=8, 16 CPUs: serial 1.189s → Ray 0.158s = 7.52x real speedup (backend=ray, speedup_claimed=true).

libroadrunner does NOT release the GIL during .simulate() (8-instance ThreadPool = 0.99x), so Ray's separate OS processes are the only path; in-process parallel_processes backfires for this CVODE-wrapping work.

studies.claim: A Ray ensemble of monoliths gives a real 7.5x wall-clock speedup on 16 cores — the one arm where vivarium wins on speed; libroadrunner does NOT release the GIL, so in-process threads cannot (they backfire).

derived.insight: n_instances=8, 16 CPUs: serial 1.189s → Ray 0.158s = 7.52x real speedup (backend=ray, speedup_claimed=true).

studies.name: arm6-coupling-demo
studies.title: Arm 6 — Cross-engine coupling demonstration
studies.question: Can a single composite run part of the model in libroadrunner and part as a native process, sharing one store — a composition a monolithic SBML model structurally cannot express?
methods: native Python/numpy Teusink RHS + scipy LSODA (lower submodel)

findings.summary: Hybrid composite: upper glycolysis (Tellurium SubmodelProcess) + lower glycolysis (NativeSubmodelProcess) share one species store, reconciling additively — a composition a single libroadrunner model cannot express.
Reproduces arm 3 (same ODEs, different engine) to max_rel_err 3.2e-7; the monolith-impossibility is STRUCTURAL, not numeric. Accuracy-exempt in the 3-way figure.

studies.claim: A single composite runs HALF in libroadrunner and HALF native, sharing one store — structurally impossible for a monolith — and reproduces the biological-seam arm to 3.2e-7. This is the composability payoff, not a numeric result.

derived.insight: Hybrid composite: upper glycolysis (Tellurium SubmodelProcess) + lower glycolysis (NativeSubmodelProcess) share one species store, reconciling additively — a composition a single libroadrunner model cannot express.

studies.name: arm7-multirate
studies.title: Arm 7 — Multi-rate scheduler stress test (process-bigraph
studies.question: When a composite is genuinely multi-rate (many independent instances each on a different coupling interval — the mismatched-interval case arms 1-6 avoid), does process-bigraph #270's event-heap scheduler reduce the per-tick O(P) due-scan to O(log P), so the many-rate run scales as ~O(P log P) instead of O(P^2) — and does it stay bit-identical to the stock scan loop?
methods: N independent libroadrunner/CVODE monolith instances (arm 1 per node)
process-bigraph #270 event-heap temporal scheduler (O(P log P))

findings.summary: Scan and heap are bit-identical at every measured P — multirate_scaling records a per-N bit_identical flag (np.array_equal of the two schedulers' final state across every instance store), True at each of P=4..256, and a dedicated test asserts it across the measured Ns (not just the small-N case). #270 changes only the order in which due processes are popped, never the math. The multi-rate composite is uncoupled (independent monoliths, empty inputs), so there is no operator-splitting divergence to confound the timing.

Measured scan vs heap run() wall-clock (median of 3, construction excluded), geometric intervals i_fast=H/(3P)..i_slow=3H, H=20: P=4 scan=0.0082s heap=0.0083s (0.98x); P=16 0.0468s / 0.0492s (0.95x); P=64 0.419s / 0.371s (1.13x); P=128 1.555s / 1.280s (1.22x); P=256 6.598s / 4.019s (1.64x). The heap/scan speedup rises monotonically with P and crosses over near P~50-64.

Honesty: heap is ~5% SLOWER at tiny P (P=4,16) — the event-heap bookkeeping has nothing to gain when the per-tick scan is trivially short — exactly #270's documented single-rate penalty. The win is modest (<=1.64x) at the P a test can afford because the real libroadrunner/CVODE update per due process dominates the per-tick Python scan at small P (measured crossover ~P=50-64). #270's cheap-process micro-benchmark (where the scheduler is the whole cost) is 4.8x@P=100 rising to 46x@P=1000; arm 7 reproduces the TREND with real integrator instances, not those multipliers.

Scheduler API used (#270): the strategy is the "scheduler" CONFIG FIELD on the Composite (Composite({"state": doc, "scheduler": "heap"|"scan"|"auto"}, core=core)); "auto" (the default) picks heap only when more than one distinct process interval is present. Arm 7 selects "scan" vs "heap" explicitly to measure both.

studies.claim: process-bigraph #270's event-heap scheduler is bit-identical to the stock scan loop (same math, different tick order) and its wall-clock advantage grows monotonically with P on a genuinely multi-rate composite — measured 0.98x at P=4 (heap bookkeeping with nothing to gain), crossing over near P~50-64, to 1.64x at P=256 on real libroadrunner/CVODE instances. The per-process CVODE integration dominates the per-tick scan until P reaches the low hundreds, so the multiplier is modest at the P a unit test can afford; it is reported as measured, and the regime where it grows large (hundreds-to-thousands of cheap processes) is #270's own 4.8x@P=100 -> 46x@P=1000 micro-benchmark, cited not reproduced.

derived.insight: Scan and heap are bit-identical at every measured P — multirate_scaling records a per-N bit_identical flag (np.array_equal of the two schedulers' final state across every instance store), True at each of P=4..256, and a dedicated test asserts it across the measured Ns (not just the small-N case). #270 changes only the order in which due processes are popped, never the math. The multi-rate composite is uncoupled (independent monoliths, empty inputs), so there is no operator-splitting divergence to confound the timing.

studies.name: arm8-multiorgan
studies.title: Arm 8 — Multi-organ scaling (where monolithic Tellurium strains)
studies.question: As an SBML model grows large (tens -> hundreds -> thousands of species), where does a monolithic libroadrunner/CVODE instance strain — in model BUILD (compile) time, in integration time, or both — and does decomposing the body into N per-organ process-bigraph sub-processes coupled through a shared store actually come out ahead end-to-end, or does it just move the cost around?
methods: single libroadrunner/CVODE instance over the whole N-organ body

findings.summary: STRONG RESULT — the monolithic libroadrunner BUILD (compile) strains superlinearly: measured medians 0.20 s at 97 species, 1.76 s at 385, 5.54 s at 769, 18.5 s at 1537 species — ~94x the build cost for ~16x the reactions (~O(N^1.64)). The dense-CVODE integration blows up alongside it (0.0023 s -> 0.058 s -> 0.395 s -> 2.56 s). Both halves of the monolithic cost grow superlinearly; this is the real, well-measured strain point and the arm's headline.

HONEST NEGATIVE — decomposition does NOT build "several-fold faster by hundreds of species". The decomposed build is N separate libroadrunner setups: SLOWER than the single monolithic compile up to ~100 species (97 sp: 0.34 s vs 0.20 s, 1.7x slower), roughly at PARITY by 385 species (1.40 vs 1.76 s), and a clear win only at ~1500 species (7.75 vs 18.5 s, 2.4x). The build crossover is at the hundreds-of-species scale, not before.

HONEST NEGATIVE (end-to-end) — the decomposed per-tick RUN overhead dwarfs the monolith's raw CVODE run: at 385 species decomp_run 0.95 s vs mono_run 0.058 s (~16x). So the decomposed body is SLOWER END-TO-END at every N measured: mono_total vs decomp_total = 0.017 vs 0.044 s (N=2), 0.039 vs 0.143 (N=8), 0.200 vs 0.559 (N=32), 1.81 vs 2.35 (N=128). The end-to-end gap narrows as N grows (3.6x -> 1.3x), but the decomposed run is UNMEASURED past N=128 (too slow for the harness), so NO end-to-end crossover is claimed. Decomposition trades the monolith's superlinear build for higher run overhead; it would only pay off end-to-end on models larger than we measured.

The coupling is genuine: Glc_blood lives in ONE shared store and every organ writes the delta it produced on it, reconciled additively through the bigraph apply path (arm-3 pattern). The shared pool drains more as more organs are added (monotone in N — a test asserts 8 organs drain it below the 2-organ case), which is only possible if the organs genuinely share the pool (contrast arm 7's N INDEPENDENT monoliths).

CRUCIAL caveat — accuracy and speed do NOT line up. The decomposed-vs-monolithic max_rel_err is a first-order additive-split error: 2e-3 at N=2, 1.2e-2 at N=8, 5.2e-2 at N=32, 0.31 (31%) at N=128. It HALVES as the coupling interval halves (verified) and GROWS with coupling density (more organs competing for the one pool per interval). The N=128 point where the end-to-end gap is smallest is exactly where accuracy (0.31) is unusable — so the speed crossover regime and the acceptable-accuracy regime do not co-occur at a fixed interval. Restoring accuracy at large N needs a finer interval, which adds more ticks and makes the decomposed run even slower. This is why the study verdict is PARTIAL.

studies.claim: The one strong, well-measured result is that the MONOLITHIC libroadrunner BUILD strains superlinearly in the reaction count: 0.20 s at 97 species -> 1.76 s at 385 -> 5.54 s at 769 -> 18.5 s at 1537 species (~94x for ~16x the reactions, ~O(N^1.64)), with the dense-CVODE run blowing up alongside it (0.0023 s -> 2.56 s). That is the real strain point and the reason a very large SBML model is painful to run monolithically. Decomposition is NOT a free win: building N small models is SLOWER than the single compile up to ~100 species (1.7x slower at 97 species), reaches only rough parity at 385 species (1.40 vs 1.76 s) and becomes a clear build win only at ~1500 species (2.4x); and the decomposed per-tick RUN overhead is ~16x the monolith's CVODE run, so the decomposed body is SLOWER END-TO-END at every N measured (decomp_total 2.35 s vs mono_total 1.81 s at 385 species). The end-to-end gap narrows with N but the decomposed run is unmeasured past N=128, so no end-to-end crossover is claimed. Decomposition is a structural trade — it swaps the monolith's superlinear build for much higher run overhead — that would only pay off end-to-end on models larger than measured. CRUCIAL caveat: the additive-split accuracy is good only at small N / fine interval (max_rel_err 2e-3 at N=2, 1.2e-2 at N=8, 5.2e-2 at N=32) and is 0.31 (31%) at N=128 — so the regime where the speed gap narrows and the regime of acceptable accuracy do NOT co-occur at a fixed coupling interval. All numbers measured, not fabricated.

derived.insight: STRONG RESULT — the monolithic libroadrunner BUILD (compile) strains superlinearly: measured medians 0.20 s at 97 species, 1.76 s at 385, 5.54 s at 769, 18.5 s at 1537 species — ~94x the build cost for ~16x the reactions (~O(N^1.64)). The dense-CVODE integration blows up alongside it (0.0023 s -> 0.058 s -> 0.395 s -> 2.56 s). Both halves of the monolithic cost grow superlinearly; this is the real, well-measured strain point and the arm's headline.

studies.name: arm9-abm-meanfield
studies.title: Arm 9 — Agent-based model vs its mean-field SBML reduction (the adversarial arm)
studies.question: The whole investigation assumes the model you start with is an SBML/ODE network. But can an AGENT-BASED model — a population of discrete individuals with stochastic interactions — even BE an SBML/Tellurium model? If you reduce it to a mean-field ODE and run it in libroadrunner/CVODE, where does that reduction hold and where does it structurally break?

findings.summary: REDUCTION VALID AT LARGE N — at population scale K=400 (80 Gillespie-SSA runs, ~2 Lotka-Volterra periods) the mean-field ODE integrated by libroadrunner/CVODE reproduces the SSA ensemble mean to a max relative error of 4.9% (mean 1.0%), and 0% of runs go extinct. This is the Kurtz large-population limit in action: at enough individuals the discrete stochastic model and its continuous deterministic SBML reduction agree, so the ABM genuinely DOES reduce to an SBML model here.

REDUCTION INVALID AT SMALL N — at scale K=8 (200 SSA runs) 94% of runs go EXTINCT before the horizon (prey or predator count hits 0, an absorbing state), while the mean-field ODE — neutrally stable closed orbits — simply cycles forever and NEVER goes extinct. The SSA ensemble mean diverges from the ODE by 68% max relative error. The deterministic SBML reduction misses the single most important qualitative behaviour of the small-population system (that it dies out).

STRUCTURAL LIMIT, NOT A TOLERANCE — the gap is not something a finer integrator or looser tolerance closes. The ODE state is (prey, predator) concentrations; it has no representation of integer discreteness, of demographic noise variance, or of the extinction probability, at ANY K. Those are properties of the ensemble and the absorbing boundary, which a single deterministic trajectory cannot carry. The ABM was NOT tuned to match the ODE — the large-N agreement and the small-N divergence are both measured.

FEASIBILITY STATEMENT — "can an ABM even be an SBML/Tellurium model?" Answer: yes, but ONLY as its large-population, well-mixed, deterministic mean-field limit. That reduction is a real, runnable SBML model (the predator_prey_meanfield composite's Antimony) and is faithful when individuals are many; it silently discards stochasticity, discreteness, extinction and individual heterogeneity, which at small population size ARE the behaviour. This is the adversarial result that breaks the naive "just decompose/rewrite any model as SBML" claim the rest of the investigation operates under.

studies.claim: An agent-based model reduces to an SBML/Tellurium mean-field ODE ONLY in the large-population, well-mixed, deterministic limit; it structurally cannot capture stochasticity, discreteness, extinction, or individual heterogeneity. MEASURED (Lotka-Volterra, base rates r=a=b=m=1, start density (1.8, 1.0), horizon ~2 periods): at a LARGE population scale K=400 (80 SSA runs) the mean-field ODE reproduces the SSA ensemble mean to a max relative error of 4.9% with 0% of runs going extinct — the reduction is VALID. At a SMALL scale K=8 (200 SSA runs) the ensemble mean diverges from the ODE by 68% max relative error and 94% of runs go EXTINCT before the horizon, hitting an absorbing state (prey or predator count 0) that the neutrally-stable ODE — which simply orbits forever — can never reach. The ODE additionally cannot represent the ensemble variance at ANY K. So "can an ABM be an SBML model?" has an honest, quantified answer: yes, but only as its large-population mean-field limit, and that reduction silently discards exactly the stochastic/discrete phenomena (extinction, demographic noise) that are often the biological point. This breaks the naive "just write it as SBML" claim.

derived.insight: REDUCTION VALID AT LARGE N — at population scale K=400 (80 Gillespie-SSA runs, ~2 Lotka-Volterra periods) the mean-field ODE integrated by libroadrunner/CVODE reproduces the SSA ensemble mean to a max relative error of 4.9% (mean 1.0%), and 0% of runs go extinct. This is the Kurtz large-population limit in action: at enough individuals the discrete stochastic model and its continuous deterministic SBML reduction agree, so the ABM genuinely DOES reduce to an SBML model here.
